analysis.one_liner: Restores discrimination lawsuits based on policy effects, bans forced arbitration, and ends qualified immunity.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it easier to win discrimination cases by allowing lawsuits over policies that have a discriminatory effect even without discriminatory intent, reversing a 2001 Supreme Court decision that limited such suits. It would also ban the forced arbitration clauses and class-action waivers that many employers and consumer businesses put in contracts, end qualified immunity as a defense for government officials sued for violating constitutional rights, and ban racial and other profiling by law enforcement. It would additionally expand civil rights protections to cover sexual orientation, gender identity, pregnancy, and natural Black hairstyles, and bar landlords from refusing tenants because of their income source, such as housing vouchers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, tenants, consumers, students, and people who face discrimination. Anyone with a forced arbitration clause in an employment or consumer contract regains access to federal and state courts, including the ability to join class actions. Victims of policies with discriminatory effects regain the right to sue, and people harmed by police profiling or by officials violating their constitutional rights get a clearer path to damages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, tenants, and consumers facing discrimination

how_it_helps.text: Restores the private right of action to challenge policies with a discriminatory effect under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, Title IX, the Age Discrimination Act, the Rehabilitation Act, and the Fair Housing Act, responding to the Supreme Court's 2001 Alexander v. Sandoval decision, which the bill's findings say stripped victims of the right to bring such suits in federal court [S3, S2].

Makes predispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers unenforceable for employment, consumer, and civil rights disputes, so individuals can take those disputes to court and participate in joint or class actions; voluntary arbitration after a dispute arises would still be allowed [S3].

Ends qualified immunity as a defense in lawsuits under the federal civil rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) and makes it easier to sue private entities performing government functions, while holding political subdivisions liable for officials' acts [S3].

Prohibits law enforcement profiling based on race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, sex, gender identity, or sexual orientation in stops, searches, and investigations, with statistical proof of disparate impact serving as prima facie evidence of a violation [S3].

Expands public accommodations protections to cover sexual orientation, gender identity, sex stereotypes, pregnancy, and natural Black hairstyles, and extends coverage to online retailers, banks, salons, transportation services, and other providers of goods and services beyond the 1964 law's original scope [S3].
Adds 'source of income' to the Fair Housing Act, barring landlords from rejecting applicants because they pay with housing vouchers, Social Security, child support, or other lawful income [S3].

Allows prevailing plaintiffs to recover compensatory and punitive damages, attorney's fees, and expert fees in discrimination cases, and removes the Faragher-Ellerth defense and the 'catalyst theory' restrictions the bill's findings say leave harassment victims without recourse [S3, S2].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses and institutions covered by the expanded rules: employers facing strict liability for workplace harassment and disparate-impact suits, landlords who screen applicants by income source, law enforcement agencies and municipal governments facing damages suits without qualified immunity, and a much wider set of consumer-facing businesses (including online retailers) subject to public accommodations law. Arbitration providers would lose a large share of their case stream.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, landlords, police, and consumer businesses

drawbacks.text: The bill extends public accommodations law to 'any establishment that provides a good, service, or program,' including online retailers, banks, salons, and health care providers, exposing a far broader range of firms, including small businesses, to federal discrimination litigation than the 1964 statute covered [S3].

The bill makes employers liable for any act of discrimination or harassment by any employee and expressly removes the defenses that the employer exercised reasonable care to prevent harassment or that the employee did not use preventive opportunities, meaning employers pay even when they had anti-harassment policies in place [S3].

The bill authorizes compensatory and punitive damages and attorney's and expert fees against covered entities, including federally funded programs, schools, and (for compensatory damages) governments, which would shift substantial litigation costs onto public institutions and ultimately taxpayers [S3].

Banning predispute arbitration in consumer disputes would return those cases to court, which generally costs businesses more in litigation and can be slower and more expensive for consumers in individual cases than arbitration, though it preserves class actions that arbitration clauses typically block.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and concrete: restored court access for millions of people whose contracts force them into arbitration, a workable tool against policies that discriminate in effect, and real remedies against police misconduct. The costs are real too: the public accommodations expansion and strict employer harassment liability are written very broadly and would raise litigation exposure for many businesses, including small ones, and damages and fees would fall partly on taxpayers. The scale of the arbitration provision alone, affecting nearly every employment and consumer contract in the country, makes this a major transfer of legal power from institutions to individuals.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Education and Labor committees the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, at which point it died.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the bill on October 27, 2020, in the final weeks of the 116th Congress, joined by Reps. Joe Kennedy and Deb Haaland as original cosponsors [S3, S5].
The bill was referred to the Committee on the Judiciary and, in addition, to the Committee on Education and Labor on the day of introduction [S5].
Only two cosponsors signed on, both House Democrats [S4].
No further action of any kind was taken after the referral; the complete action history shows only the introduction and the committee referrals [S5].
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without either chamber voting on it [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that use forced arbitration clauses, employers facing harassment and disparate-impact exposure, landlords who decline voucher holders, and law enforcement agencies protected by qualified immunity all kept the existing legal rules, since the bill died without a hearing or vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Arbitration-using businesses and agencies kept the status quo

industries.industry: Forced arbitration and class-action-waiver users (employers and consumer businesses)
industries.note: The bill makes predispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers unenforceable in employment, consumer, and civil rights disputes, ending the industry-wide practice of routing these cases to private arbitration where class actions are barred. Their gain under current law is individuals' loss of court access, which is why the bill targets the practice directly [S3].
A ban on predispute arbitration clauses in the largest categories of disputes would eliminate much of the consumer and employment arbitration caseload these firms process [S3].
Strict vicarious liability for any employee's harassment, removal of the Faragher-Ellerth defense, and a statutory disparate-impact standard increase employer exposure across the economy [S3].

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies and municipal governments
industries.note: Eliminating qualified immunity, allowing local governments to be held liable for officers' acts, and banning profiling with damages remedies materially increase these agencies' legal and financial exposure [S3].
Adding 'source of income' to the Fair Housing Act ends the common practice of refusing tenants who pay with vouchers or other assistance income, which affects low-income renters' housing access [S3].

industries.industry: Consumer-facing businesses (retail, online retail, banking, salons, transportation, health care providers)
industries.note: The public accommodations expansion covers 'any establishment that provides a good, service, or program,' bringing firms far beyond the 1964 statute's scope into federal discrimination law [S3].
Mandatory attorney's and expert fees, damages for disparate-impact claims, and a much larger universe of actionable claims would expand the market for civil rights litigation [S3].
